extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of The Spectator; writers and readers interested in taste, manners, translation, and poetic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and critical criteria for travel, manners, theatre attendance, translation, love-writing, and epic poetry as presented in The Spectator essays (Addison & Steele).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding before travelling (avoid superficial travel)
rubrics_metrics.description: How can any of these Advantages be attained by one who is a mere Stranger to the Customs and Policies of his native Country, and has not yet fixed in his Mind the first Principles of Manners and Behaviour? To endeavour it, is to build a gawdy Structure without any Foundation; or, if I may be allow'd the Expression, to work a rich Embroidery upon a Cobweb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel undertaken without prior acquaintance with one's native customs and the first principles of manners is pointless and may produce merely ornamental, unstable effects. Implicit: acquire basic cultural/moral grounding at home before attempting to refine taste by travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel to improve taste for classical authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving our Taste of the best Authors of Antiquity, by seeing the Places where they lived, and of which they wrote; to compare the natural Face of the Country with the Descriptions they have given us, and observe how well the Picture agrees with the Original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use travel as a way to compare textual description with the actual landscape/scene, making the reading of ancient authors a 'most charming Exercise.' Also use observations of ruins to draw moral conclusions about the uncertainty of human things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine celebrated particular sites to inspire virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A nearer View of any such Particular, tho really little and trifling in it self, may serve the more powerfully to warm a generous Mind to an Emulation of their Virtues, and a greater Ardency of Ambition to imitate their bright Examples, if it comes duly temper'd and prepar'd for the Impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, local particulars (footsteps, ruins, sites associated with historical figures) can powerfully morally and aesthetically affect a prepared mind; the emotional/imaginative effect depends on prior preparation and disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid travelling too young or ignorant (warning about lasting effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: though to be Sea-sick, or jumbled in an outlandish Stage-Coach, may perhaps be healthful for the Constitution of the Body, yet it is apt to cause such a Dizziness in young empty Heads, as too often lasts their Life-time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against sending inexperienced youths abroad: physical discomforts and the novelty of travel can produce lasting mental frivolity or disorientation. Practical implication: delay certain travels until maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal conduct and preservations of virtue (advice to women in May)
rubrics_metrics.description: I design this Paper for a Caveat to the Fair Sex... That though she would promise to be chaste in every Month besides, she could not engage for her self in May... In the first place, I would advise them never to venture abroad in the Fields, but in the Company of a Parent, a Guardian, or some other sober discreet Person... In the second place, I cannot but approve those Prescriptions, which our Astrological Physicians give in their Almanacks for this Month; such as are a spare and simple Diet, with the moderate Use of Phlebotomy... I shall also advise my fair Readers to be in a particular manner careful how they meddle with Romances, Chocolate, Novels, and the like Inflamers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, period prescriptions to avoid seasonal temptations: avoid solitary excursions into fields, keep sober company, adopt spare/simple diet, consider medical/astrological precautions (phlebotomy), and refrain from stimulating entertainments and literature (romances, chocolate, novels) during the 'dangerous' month. Also: if staying in town, prefer tragic entertainments to comic/operatic ones during this season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer tragedy and moderation in entertainments when virtue is a concern
rubrics_metrics.description: As for that Part of the Fair-Sex who stay in Town, I would advise them to be particularly cautious how they give themselves up to their most innocent Entertainments. If they cannot forbear the Play-house, I would recommend Tragedy to them, rather than Comedy; and should think the Puppet-show much safer for them than the Opera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moral seriousness is desired, choose entertainments that temper mirth with severity (tragedy) or are less sensually stimulating (puppet-show) rather than comedic or operatic amusements. This is framed as protective advice for virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: In depicting love, avoid wit; let sentiment arise organically
rubrics_metrics.description: There are such wild Inconsistencies in the Thoughts of a Man in love... In Performances of this kind, the most absurd of all things is to be witty; every Sentiment must grow out of the Occasion, and be suitable to the Circumstances of the Character. Where this Rule is transgressed, the humble Servant, in all the fine things he says, is but shewing his Mistress how well he can dress, instead of saying how well he loves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing passion (especially in dramatic or poetic characters), do not sacrifice sincerity for cleverness: wit that does not arise naturally from circumstance undermines authenticity. Character-appropriate expression is essential; ornamentation that draws attention to the speaker's skill is a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's fidelity to sentiment with appropriate metrical adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: I have faithfully kept to the Sentiments, without adding or diminishing; and pretend to no greater Praise from my Translation, than they who smooth and clean the Furs of that Country which have suffered by Carriage... The Numbers in the Original are as loose and unequal... I have ventured to bind it in stricter Measures, as being more proper for our Tongue, tho perhaps wilder Graces may better suit the Genius of the Laponian Language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle for translations: preserve the original sentiments faithfully (no addition or diminution), while adapting form and meter to suit the target language — accepting that some native 'wild graces' may be restrained to fit English prosody. State the translator's limitations honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic/epic poem should end happily (poetic judgement on fable/conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: I hinted ... that an Heroick Poem, according to the Opinion of the best Criticks, ought to end happily, and leave the Mind of the Reader, after having conducted it through many Doubts and Fears, Sorrows and Disquietudes, in a State of Tranquility and Satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical standard for epic/heroic poetry: conclude in a way that reconciles and comforts the reader — even when the subject contains great adversity — so the work ultimately restores tranquility and satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit rather than narrate when possible in poetry (show vivid scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton, after having represented in Vision the History of Mankind to the first great Period of Nature, dispatches the remaining part of it in Narration... I could wish, however, that the Author had done it, whatever Pains it might have cost him. To give my Opinion freely, I think that the exhibiting part of the History of Mankind in Vision, and part in Narrative, is as if an History-Painter should put in Colours one half of his Subject, and write down the remaining part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer vivid exhibition (dramatic, pictorial representation) to mere narration for parts of a poetic work intended to move the imagination; excessive reliance on narration can dilute poetic force. Use visible objects and scenes where the subject admits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subordinating poetry to didactic/theological attention at the expense of poetic art
rubrics_metrics.description: If Milton's Poem flags any where, it is in this Narration, where in some places the Author has been so attentive to his Divinity, that he has neglected his Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet's strong preoccupation with doctrinal or theological concerns must not override poetic craft; balance is required so that theological exposition does not weaken poetic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use noble and appropriate allusion and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The River-Dragon is an Allusion to the Crocodile... This Allusion is taken from that Sublime Passage in Ezekiel... Milton has given us another very noble and poetical Image in the same Description...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ elevated, well-chosen allusions (scriptural or classical) and vivid images to strengthen poetic description. Such images should be fitting to the subject and enhance the reader's apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document exemplary conduct in detail to teach moral lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: It would certainly be of singular Use to human Society to have an exact Account of this Lady's ordinary Conduct, which was Crowned by so uncommon Magnanimity... Her Behaviour was so magnanimous throughout this whole Affair, that I was particularly curious in taking Notice of what passed as her Fate approached nearer and nearer, and took Notes of what she said to all about her, particularly Word for Word what she spoke to Mr. Festeau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offering moral exemplars, give close, faithful accounts (including verbatim speech where possible) of ordinary conduct to show how habitual virtues produce heroic moments; such detailed documentation increases the educational value of the anecdote.
